MHHS2401 · Week 5 · Blood Vessels & Lymphatics of the Upper Limb · Dr Mirjana Strkalj

Upper limb blood supply — one artery, renamed five times

A single arterial highway runs from the chest to the fingertips, changing its name at each anatomical landmark: subclavian → axillary → brachial → radial & ulnar → the palmar arches. This guide follows that highway and its branches, then traces blood back out through the superficial and deep veins and the lymphatic vessels — ending at the axillary lymph nodes, the great clinical crossroads of the upper limb.

Covers arteries, veins & lymphatics (LO1–5) Figures 5 plates from the lecture Recall 8 section checklists

§0Orientation · LO1

The arterial highway

The same vessel, renamed at each landmark.

The key to upper-limb arteries is that it is essentially one continuous artery that changes name as it passes anatomical landmarks. Learn the landmarks and the names follow.

The main arterial pathway and its name-changes
ArteryBecomes the next artery at…
Subclavianthe lateral margin of rib 1 → axillary artery
Axillarythe inferior margin of teres major → brachial artery
Brachialthe cubital fossa (neck of radius) → splits into radial & ulnar
Radial & Ulnarthe hand → superficial & deep palmar arches
Reasoning · why anastomoses matter

At every major joint (scapula, elbow, wrist/hand) the branches form anastomoses — vessels that rejoin, creating alternative routes for blood. This is not decorative: it means blood can bypass a joint even when the main vessel is kinked by movement or blocked, keeping the distal limb perfused. The scapular and elbow anastomoses and the two palmar arches are the classic examples.

Memory hook · the name-change landmarks

Rib 1 → Subclavian becomes Axillary; teres major → Axillary becomes Brachial; cubital fossa → Brachial splits into Radial + Ulnar.

R Recall checklist — the arterial highway
  • Order — subclavian → axillary → brachial → radial & ulnar → palmar arches.
  • Name-changes — lateral border of rib 1; inferior border of teres major; cubital fossa.
  • Anastomoses — at scapula, elbow and hand give collateral (bypass) routes.
§1The gateway

The axilla

The pyramidal passageway between thorax and arm.

The axilla (armpit) is a pyramidal space at the junction of the arm and thorax. It is the passageway through which the vessels, nerves and lymphatics reach the upper limb — so its walls are worth knowing because everything important travels through it.

Boundaries of the axilla
BoundaryFormed by
ApexThe entrance from the neck to the axilla
BaseSkin, subcutaneous tissue and axillary fascia
Anterior wallPectoralis major & minor
Posterior wallScapula & subscapularis; the posterior axillary fold is teres major + latissimus dorsi
Medial wallThoracic wall & serratus anterior
Lateral wallHumerus (intertubercular groove)
Reasoning · why a pyramid, and why it matters

The axilla is where the neurovascular bundle transfers from the trunk to the free limb, so it must be a protected but mobile corridor. Its contents — the axillary artery and vein, the cords of the brachial plexus, and the axillary lymph nodes — all run through this one space. That concentration is why a single lesion or a spreading cancer in the axilla can knock out blood supply, nerve supply and lymphatic drainage together.

R Recall checklist — the axilla
  • Shape/role — pyramidal space; passageway for vessels, nerves & lymphatics to the limb.
  • Walls — anterior: pec major/minor; posterior: scapula/subscapularis (fold = teres major + lat dorsi); medial: serratus anterior; lateral: humerus.
  • Contents — axillary artery & vein, brachial plexus cords, axillary lymph nodes.
§2Artery 2 · LO1

Axillary artery

Three parts, defined by pectoralis minor.

The subclavian artery becomes the axillary artery at the lateral margin of rib 1 and passes through the axilla, becoming the brachial artery at the inferior margin of teres major. Its branches are grouped into three parts — and the divider is pectoralis minor. Plate 2.1 lays them out.

Axillary artery branches by part (relative to pectoralis minor)
PartPositionBranch(es)
1stProximal to pec minorSuperior thoracic artery (1)
2ndPosterior to pec minorThoraco-acromial & lateral thoracic arteries (2)
3rdDistal to pec minorAnterior & posterior circumflex humeral, and subscapular arteries (3)
Reasoning · why so many branches here — the scapular anastomosis

The 3rd-part branches (subscapular → circumflex scapular, plus the circumflex humeral vessels) all converge around the scapula and shoulder. Together with branches of the subclavian they build the scapular anastomosis — a rich collateral network. Its purpose: the shoulder is the most mobile joint in the body, so a single artery would repeatedly kink; the anastomosis means if the axillary artery is slowly occluded between the thyrocervical trunk and the subscapular artery, blood can still reach the arm around the scapula.

Memory hook · 1-2-3 branches, and their names

The parts give 1, 2, 3 branches. Screw The Lawyer, Save A Patient — Superior thoracic · Thoraco-acromial, Lateral thoracic · Subscapular, Anterior & Posterior circumflex humeral.

Clinical · the circumflex humeral vessels

The posterior circumflex humeral artery winds around the surgical neck of the humerus (through the quadrangular space, with the axillary nerve). This makes both the vessel and the nerve vulnerable in surgical-neck fractures and shoulder dislocations — a recurring theme you'll meet again with the axillary nerve.

R Recall checklist — axillary artery
  • Start/end — lateral margin of rib 1 → inferior margin of teres major.
  • Divider — pectoralis minor splits it into 3 parts giving 1, 2, 3 branches.
  • Branches — superior thoracic; thoraco-acromial + lateral thoracic; subscapular + anterior/posterior circumflex humeral.
§3Artery 3 · LO1

Brachial artery & the cubital fossa

The main supply to the arm, ending at the elbow.

The brachial artery is the main blood supply to the arm. It begins at the inferior border of teres major and ends in the cubital fossa, opposite the neck of the radius, where it divides into the radial and ulnar arteries. Its main branches are the profunda brachii (deep artery of the arm) and the superior and inferior ulnar collateral arteries, which feed the anastomosis around the elbow.

Boundaries of the cubital fossa (triangular, anterior elbow)
BoundaryFormed by
Superior (base)Imaginary line between the medial & lateral humeral epicondyles
MedialPronator teres
LateralBrachioradialis
Clinical · the brachial pulse & blood pressure

In the cubital fossa the brachial artery lies medial to the biceps tendon and between the median and ulnar nerves' territory — this is where the stethoscope goes to auscultate Korotkoff sounds when measuring blood pressure, and where the brachial pulse is felt. Because it is the sole main channel to the forearm, a laceration or compression here threatens the whole distal limb.

Reasoning · why collateral branches at the elbow

The elbow bends through a wide arc, and a single straight artery crossing it would kink and occlude at full flexion. The ulnar collateral and profunda brachii branches loop around the joint to meet recurrent branches from the forearm arteries, forming the anastomosis around the elbow — so blood reaches the forearm at every joint angle, and can bypass a blocked brachial artery below the profunda.

R Recall checklist — brachial artery
  • Role — main supply to the arm; teres major → cubital fossa (neck of radius).
  • Branches — profunda brachii; superior & inferior ulnar collateral (elbow anastomosis).
  • Cubital fossa — base = intercondylar line; medial = pronator teres; lateral = brachioradialis; BP/pulse site.
§4Arteries 4 · LO1

Radial & ulnar arteries

The forearm's two terminal branches.

In the cubital fossa the brachial artery splits into the radial (lateral) and ulnar (medial) arteries, which run down the forearm to supply it and reach the hand. Plate 4.1 shows the split and the recurrent/interosseous branches that feed the elbow anastomosis.

Label Key — the forearm arteries
Radial artery
Runs laterally; its recurrent branch feeds the elbow. Its pulse is felt at the wrist (lateral).
Ulnar artery
Runs medially; gives anterior & posterior ulnar recurrent branches.
Interosseous arteries
The common interosseous gives anterior and posterior interosseous arteries along the interosseous membrane.
Reasoning · two arteries plus a shared membrane

Splitting into two vessels that run down opposite sides of the forearm is itself a form of redundancy — and the interosseous arteries add a third channel down the middle, on the interosseous membrane, supplying the deep muscles and linking the two sides. So the forearm is served by radial, ulnar and interosseous routes that interconnect at the elbow (recurrents) and the hand (arches), giving robust flow at every joint angle.

Clinical · the radial pulse & Allen's test

The radial artery at the wrist is the classic pulse point and the site for arterial blood sampling and lines. Before cannulating it, Allen's test checks that the ulnar artery can supply the hand via the palmar arches — a direct clinical use of the anastomosis in §5. Because the two arteries join in the hand, one can supply the whole hand if the other is compromised.

R Recall checklist — radial & ulnar arteries
  • Origin — brachial artery bifurcates in the cubital fossa.
  • Radial = lateral (wrist pulse); ulnar = medial.
  • Branches — recurrent branches (elbow anastomosis) + anterior/posterior interosseous arteries.
§5The hand · LO1

Palmar arches

Where radial and ulnar arteries rejoin.

In the hand the radial and ulnar arteries reconnect as two palmar arches, from which the digital arteries arise. Plate 5.1 shows both.

The two palmar arches
Superficial palmar archDeep palmar arch
Mainly fromUlnar arteryRadial artery
PositionMore distal (superficial)More proximal (deep)
Gives rise toCommon → proper palmar digital arteriesPrinceps pollicis, radial artery of index; deep metacarpals
Reasoning · why two arches, and why it's safe to sample the radial

Because the ulnar and radial arteries both feed the arches, the hand has a double, cross-connected supply: block or sample one artery and the other keeps the hand alive through the arches. This dual supply is precisely why the radial artery can be safely cannulated at the wrist (after a normal Allen's test) — the ulnar side covers the hand meanwhile.

R Recall checklist — palmar arches
  • Superficial arch — mainly ulnar artery; more distal.
  • Deep arch — mainly radial artery; more proximal.
  • Digital supply — arches → common → proper palmar digital arteries; cross-connection protects the hand.
§6Drainage · LO2

Venous drainage

Two systems: superficial veins and deep venae comitantes.

Blood returns via two sets of veins. Plate 6.1 shows the superficial system, the one you can see and cannulate.

Superficial vs deep veins
Superficial veinsDeep veins
LocationIn the superficial fasciaDeep to the deep fascia
PatternVariable; do not accompany arteriesAccompany arteries, usually as paired venae comitantes
ValvesFewerMore valves than superficial
Named veinsCephalic, basilic, median cubitalPaired veins alongside brachial/radial/ulnar arteries
Reasoning · why pair a vein with an artery? (venae comitantes)

A vena comitans is a vein wrapped around a smaller artery as a pair. The point is mechanical: the arterial pulse squeezes the adjacent veins with every beat, and the valves force that squeeze to pump blood back toward the heart — the pulse itself aids venous return. Superficial veins, having no artery to pump them, rely more on muscle action.

Clinical · the median cubital vein

The median cubital vein crosses the cubital fossa, connecting cephalic and basilic veins. Superficial, large and relatively fixed, it is the standard site for venepuncture and IV access — which is exactly why knowing that the brachial artery and median nerve lie just deep to it (behind the bicipital aponeurosis) matters for safe needle placement.

R Recall checklist — venous drainage
  • Superficial — cephalic (lateral), basilic (medial), median cubital (connects them); fewer valves; don't follow arteries.
  • Deep — venae comitantes accompanying the arteries in pairs; more valves; the pulse aids return.
  • Clinical — median cubital vein = venepuncture; brachial artery/median nerve lie deep to it.
§7Drainage · LO3

Lymphatic drainage

All roads lead to the axillary nodes.

Lymph follows two sets of vessels — superficial (skin & subcutaneous tissue) and deep (accompanying the deep arteries and veins) — and both converge on the axillary lymph nodes. Plate 7.1 shows the five groups and the order in which lymph passes through them.

The five axillary node groups
GroupDrains…
1 · Pectoral (anterior)Anterior thoracic wall & breast
2 · Subscapular (posterior)Posterior thoracic wall & scapular region
3 · Humeral (lateral)Most of the upper limb (except vessels around the cephalic vein)
4 · CentralReceives from groups 1–3; lies deep to pectoralis minor
5 · ApicalReceives from central (and cephalic-vein vessels) → subclavian trunk
Reasoning · the drainage sequence

The order is not arbitrary — it funnels. The three peripheral groups (pectoral, subscapular, humeral) drain into the central nodes, which drain into the apical nodes at the apex, which empty via the subclavian lymphatic trunk into the right lymphatic duct (right side) or the thoracic duct (left side), and thence to the venous system. Learn it as a pyramid emptying upward toward the neck.

Clinical · breast cancer & palpating nodes

Because the pectoral group drains the breast, the axillary nodes are the first site of spread for breast cancer, and axillary node status is central to staging. Clinically, lymph nodes are palpated at three main sites — cervical, axillary and inguinal. Enlarged axillary nodes (lymphadenopathy) point to disease in the breast, thoracic wall or upper limb they drain.

R Recall checklist — lymphatic drainage
  • Two vessel sets — superficial (skin) & deep (with arteries/veins) → axillary nodes.
  • Five groups — pectoral, subscapular, humeral → central → apical.
  • Exit — apical → subclavian trunk → right lymphatic duct (R) / thoracic duct (L).
  • Clinical — pectoral group drains the breast (cancer staging); palpate cervical/axillary/inguinal.

Week 5 (blood supply) in one line. One arterial highway — subclavian → axillary (3 parts, split by pec minor) → brachial (main arm supply, ends in the cubital fossa) → radial & ulnar → the superficial & deep palmar arches — with anastomoses at every joint for collateral flow; blood returns via superficial veins (cephalic, basilic, median cubital) and deep venae comitantes; and lymph funnels through the pectoral, subscapular, humeral, central and apical axillary nodes to the subclavian trunk.
